articles.title: How England's Max King turned Rugby League World Cup dream into reality: 'I had it written on a sticky note on my wall'
articles.summary: England's Max King is living out a dream he has had for a long time when he represents England at the Rugby League World Cup; He qualifies for England as he was born in Huddersfield and his mother is English
articles.body:
King was born in Huddersfield and moved over to Australia at seven years of age, meaning his early memories of rugby league were his grandfather's affiliation with Leeds Rhinos and Huddersfield's love for the sport.

The Canterbury Bulldogs prop has had World Cup ambitions for a long time and had a sticky note on his wall to try and make the England side for the World Cup four years ago in 2022.

While that dream did not occur at that particular moment, a phone call from new England head coach Brian McDermott reignited the ambition for King that sees him in the squad for this year's World Cup at which he will represent his own and his mother's English heritage.

From that phone call, the dream that once was physically represented as a sticky note on his bedroom wall was now alive and about to become a reality, if selected for England in their opening match against Tonga on Saturday October 17.

"I was born and raised in Huddersfield. I can still remember being a seven-year-old but I have been back and forth a number of times with my mum's side of the family," King said.

"So I've been a couple of times you know as a teenager, as a sort of young adult.

"I grew up around league, I know obviously it's football mad you know, but I grew up as a league family and yeah I remember going to the Leeds Rhinos games. My grandfather was a Leeds Rhinos tragic.

"It is a special moment for my family being able to represent myself and my heritage.

"My dad was just as ecstatic as everyone else and my mum was quite emotional. My parents have always been supportive and they'd be supportive for me if I was playing for a local third grade side.

"I was sharing a story with a couple of boys last night. I like to write goals on the wall and sort of sticky note them and my wife reminds me when we first started dating. She came over to my house and I had this big sticky note that was across from my bed.

"I would see it every day and the was a goal to make the World Cup for the England side in 2022.

"Unfortunately, it wasn't to be and I kind of thought from there that it just wasn't going to happen you know and I think sometimes you know being on the Australian side it can sometimes be harder just because your loyalty and dedication towards England probably gets questioned.

"It wasn't until Brian McDermott gave me a call this year and asked me how I felt about the opportunity to play and I was buzzing.

"I was just trying to make sure I was doing whatever it took to to be here towards the end of the year and have this opportunity alongside some of the boys.

"Spending time with Brian, the limited time that I have, he is definitely an emotional speaker and he can definitely get the hairs on the back of the neck to stand up at times.

"Obviously, that dream that I had reignited and it didn't take much."

'The English boys will become mates for life'

King knows some of the England group but with the majority of them playing in Super League, they are names he has heard and faces he recognises rather than people he knows.

However, King thinks the "English culture" has meant he has been embraced immediately, something he knew would happen thanks to anecdotes from his dad.

King's dad, David, played for Huddersfield Giants and let his son know, once in the English environment, he will come away with friends for life.

"It's definitely a new group and that can be daunting. Sometimes that stuff takes a couple weeks to gel and feel at home but I feel like the boys have really welcomed me with open arms," he added.

"I think that's an English culture to be honest. I remember asking my dad a couple months ago.

"He played a bit in NRL, but he played most of his career in the Super League and I said what was the difference and the biggest thing he said was just the English culture the mateship for having your back.

"He said that he has mates from footy in Australia but the blokes he played with in England they were mates for the rest of his life.

"He still speaks to them to this day and that really inspired me.

"I can't fault the boys. They are so easy and great to get along with.

"We have had some bonding sessions, but the boys are full of laughs and great to be around so I feel right at home."

images.caption: Image: Max King will get to live out his dream when he represents England at the Rugby League World Cup

articles.title: Manchester United: Viral clip shows Spurs beat the press at Old Trafford - and exposes other issues
articles.summary: Man Utd have made their worst start to a league season in 40 years; Saturday's 1-1 draw with 10-man Spurs generated a viral clip of Michael Carrick's side being opened up by a pass out from the back but it also highlights midfield and intensity problems the United boss has to solve
articles.body:
The 10-second clip has become a lightning rod for fan frustrations.

United's return of six points from six Premier League games is the fewest they've gained at this stage of a season in 40 years - and right now, every shortcoming is being heavily scrutinised.

But what does the clip, and other similiar instances in the game, reveal about Manchester United?

The clip occurs in the 57th minute. The score is 0-0. Jan Paul van Hecke has the ball in the Spurs penalty area after receiving a short goal-kick from centre-back partner Marco Senesi.

Six United players have stepped up and gone man-to-man to deploy a high press. But their four defenders are back on the halfway line, leaving a big gap between the United defence and midfield.

Crucially, United's left winger, Matheus Cunha, is stood too far away from Spurs right-back Archie Gray. Van Hecke is closed down but is able to make a straightforward pass into Gray's path. Gray is already on the charge into the space in front of United's defence.

With one pass out of their own penalty area, Spurs have left six United players trailing behind the ball. Carrick can be seen gesturing to Cunha to chase back - but Gray is away.

Gray is able to carry the ball all the way to United's defensive third where he plays a square pass to the unmarked Conor Gallagher. United's central midfielders, Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo, are running back but can't make up the ground in time.

"If you look at Tielemans and Mainoo getting back here, the two in midfield chasing back, it's a real struggle for them," says Sky Sports' Gary Neville on co-commentary.

Gallagher shuttles the ball onto Spurs left winger Savio, who takes a touch and then sees his shot blocked out for a corner by Leny Yoro.

The clip comes in the context of United already suffering criticism this season for their fitness, intensity out of possession and compactness.

"When you come back from the World Cup, you don't do lots of running. Just chill." That was the quote from Tielemans to Rio Ferdinand in pre-season when he was asked about training under Carrick in preparation for the upcoming campaign.

It has been repeatedly referenced in these opening weeks given United have been out-run in every Premier League fixture so far, aside from the Manchester derby, when Man City had Phil Foden sent off in the first half.

Cunha himself said after the draw at Fulham before the international break: "They put in more energy than us, we cannot accept this."

Neville was scathing of that showing from United and on Saturday he was critical of the Tielemans-Mainoo partnership being energetic enough for the Premier League.

Summer signing Carlos Baleba, who has seen his start at the club disrupted by injury, came on as a substitute for Tielemans after United defended two Spurs corners which followed the viral clip. Could he provide the solution now he is returning to fitness?

Perhaps - but the answer surely also requires a more joined-up approach from United's players out of possession which doesn't require a player to cover huge areas of grass on their own to prevent teams gaining huge territory as quickly and easily as Spurs did on Saturday.

While one clip went viral, there are other examples of United's defensive set-up being stretched.

Just 12 minutes into the match, Spurs had their first goal-kick. Again they went short, with Senesi passing to goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky. Left-back Destiny Udogie was quickly on the run, realising Amad Diallo had given him space and was looking the other way.

It was a near-identical situation to the Gray incident which would happen later in the match. But on this occasion, Senesi turns back and declines to make the pass out to Udogie, who had raced into space behind the United midfield.

United's front six disconnect from the rest

The viral clip wasn't the only occasion when United allowed a huge gap to open up between their defence and the rest of the team.

Seven minutes before Gray is released, Bruno Fernandes closes down Kinsky to prevent him from passing to Van Hecke. But the plan from Spurs is there and so is the opportunity provided by the big space behind Tielemans and Mainoo.

United's Cunha looks like he is blowing a minute before the viral incident, when Kinsky opts to go long.

Fatigue could be a factor in United being unable to effectively deploy their man-to-man high press - especially considering that Cunha gives Gray too much space soon after this screenshot, which allows Spurs to break up the pitch.

Into the 87th minute, and with United 1-0 up there is more caution in Cunha's positioning. The Brazilian is deeper than in previous set-ups for Spurs goal-kicks and is able to deny Van Hecke the option of playing a similar pass for Gray as previously.

However, five other United players have pushed up on their opponents - leaving that space in behind them again. Remember, United have a one-goal lead against 10 men with less than four minutes of normal time remaining.

Fortunately, United have Baleba on the pitch, who has spotted the passing option for Van Hecke...

Baleba charges across the pitch to make the interception just in time.

United scrambled to survive on that occasion. But ultimately they did concede an injury-time equaliser - fuelling more scrutiny of United's approach and performances this season.

articles.title: La 'resurrección' de Isco Alarcón
articles.standfirst: El malagueño, decisivo ante Osasuna con un doblete, empieza a dejar atrás su calvario
articles.summary: El malagueño, decisivo ante Osasuna con un doblete, empieza a dejar atrás su calvario
articles.body: Cuando el Betis anunció el fichaje de Isco Alarcón, en julio de 2023, recurrió a una de las escenas más famosas de Juego de Tronos: la resurrección de Jon Nieve. En aquel vídeo, inspirado en la popular serie de televisión, el malagueño volvía a la vida después de una etapa complicada en su carrera, dispuesto a recuperar el fútbol que llevaba dentro. Más de tres años después, aquella presentación parece haber adquirido un significado casi premonitorio. Porque Isco, que ya había conseguido renacer futbolísticamente de la mano de Manuel Pellegrini, ha tenido que volver a hacerlo. Esta vez, después de un auténtico calvario de lesiones, operaciones y dolores que llegaron a sembrar dudas sobre su futuro. Su exhibición frente a Osasuna en la tarde de ayer en La Cartuja, con dos goles decisivos para que el Betis sumara tres nuevos puntos y prolongara su extraordinario arranque de temporada, fue la confirmación de que el camino recorrido ha merecido la pena para el capitán bético. Isco vuelve a sonreír sobre el césped, a disfrutar con el balón y a marcar diferencias. Y los números empiezan a reflejar una recuperación que va mucho más allá de las sensaciones. En apenas ocho jornadas de Liga y un partido de Champions, el mediapunta acumula 462 minutos repartidos en nueve encuentros oficiales, exactamente los mismos partidos que disputó durante toda la pasada temporada en la que las lesiones limitaron su participación a sólo 236 minutos. Es decir, prácticamente el doble de tiempo sobre el terreno de juego. También ha triplicado sus titularidades, pasando de dos a seis, y ha mejorado sus registros ofensivos: dos goles y una asistencia, frente a un tanto y un pase de gol en todo el curso anterior. Tres participaciones directas en goles frente a dos. Para entender el valor de esta nueva versión de Isco hay que remontarse a mayo de 2024. Cuando había recuperado su mejor nivel con el Betis y se había ganado el derecho a soñar con disputar la Eurocopa, una fractura de peroné frente a Las Palmas lo dejó fuera de combate. Tuvo que pasar por el quirófano y, ante las dificultades en la consolidación del hueso, someterse a una segunda intervención meses después. No pudo disputar el torneo continental que terminaría conquistando España y permaneció siete meses alejado de los terrenos de juego. Regresó en diciembre de aquel año y protagonizó una segunda mitad de temporada extraordinaria, liderando al Betis hasta la primera final europea de su historia. El fútbol volvía a sonreírle y se le abrían de nuevo las puertas de la Selección para disputar una Nations League que al combinado dirigido por Luis de la Fuente se le escapó en los penaltis ante Portugal. Pero cuando parecía haber dejado definitivamente atrás aquella pesadilla, el drama de las lesiones volvió a golpearlo con dureza. En agosto de 2025, durante el último amistoso de pretemporada frente a su querido Málaga en La Rosaleda, una entrada de David Larrubia le provocó una nueva fractura de peroné. Otra lesión grave, en la misma zona que había sufrido un año antes, pero sin relación con la anterior, que estaba completamente curada tal y como explicaron en su día los servicios médicos del club. Un nuevo contratiempo que le impidió comenzar la temporada con su equipo y lo mantuvo apartado durante más de tres meses. Reapareció en noviembre frente al Girona, con la mente puesta en jugar el derbi de la semana siguiente. Pero la alegría apenas le duró cuatro días. En su siguiente encuentro, ante el Utrecht en la fase de liga de la Europa League, un desafortunado choque con su compañero Sofyan Amrabat le provocó una grave lesión en el tobillo derecho, con afectación del cartílago. Los médicos apostaron inicialmente por un tratamiento conservador, pero los dolores persistían y finalmente tuvo que someterse a una nueva intervención quirúrgica. Fueron meses de incertidumbre, de dificultades para avanzar en la recuperación y de molestias que complicaban incluso los gestos más habituales de un futbolista. El estado del cartílago y la persistencia del dolor alimentaron las dudas sobre cuándo podría volver a competir al máximo nivel. Y no solo eso, como él mismo confesó después, la incógnita alcanzó incluso a la posibilidad de que no pudiera volver a jugar al fútbol de élite. El trabajo realizado durante el verano resultó fundamental para comenzar a dejar atrás aquellas molestias. Isco pudo completar la pretemporada con el grupo, recuperar progresivamente sensaciones y fortalecer un tobillo que llevaba demasiado tiempo condicionando su rendimiento. Pellegrini y su cuerpo técnico han administrado cuidadosamente sus esfuerzos, conscientes de la importancia de evitar sobrecargas después de un periodo tan prolongado de inactividad. Y el reciente parón de tres semanas a finales de septiembre y principios de octubre por los compromisos internacionales de selecciones ha supuesto otro impulso importante para el 22. Sin la exigencia de los partidos, el malagueño ha podido profundizar en su preparación física en los entrenamientos diarios con sus compañeros y dar un nuevo paso hacia su mejor versión. Una versión que ya pudo verse ayer en el partido ante el conjunto rojillo. "Contento, cada vez con más ritmo. Estas tres semanas me han dado tiempo para trabajar y ponerme a punto, que todavía me falta, pero trabajando con mucha ilusión, con muchas ganas de mejorar, de ayudar al equipo y se nos presenta una temporada muy ilusionante", reconocía en los micrófonos de Movistar LaLiga TV después de ser elegido mejor jugador del partido frente a Osasuna. Su doblete fue determinante. Primero abrió el marcador desde el punto de penalti y después apareció para firmar el 4-2 cuando Osasuna, que había llegado a perder por tres goles, amenazaba con completar una remontada inesperada. Pero su influencia en el juego fue mucho más allá de las dos acciones que terminaron en gol. Según los datos de Opta, Isco completó 41 de los 43 pases que intentó, con un 95,3% de precisión, y firmó 16 pases progresivos. En los 74 minutos que disputó acumuló seis remates, ganó dos duelos y recuperó cinco balones, sin registrar pérdidas de balón. Una actuación que reflejó tanto su capacidad para desequilibrar en los últimos metros como su creciente protagonismo en la elaboración del juego, bajando al centro del campo a recibir entre los pivotes para dar salida a las jugadas de su equipo poniendo orden y visión de juego. El Betis, poco a poco, vuelve a encontrar en él a ese futbolista capaz de interpretar cada jugada, manejar los tiempos y aparecer cuando el equipo más lo necesita. "Después de un montón de rebotes ahí en el área, he ido con fe, me ha caído el balón y he metido un gol importante porque se nos había puesto muy complicado. Ellos estaban apretando mucho y estoy contento sobre todo por la victoria", explicó sobre su segundo tanto, que trajo la calma a un Betis que había perdido el control de la situación ante los de Luis Miguel Ramis después de recibir dos goles prácticamente seguidos que apretaban el marcador. El entrenador chileno, que ha sido fundamental en las distintas etapas de recuperación futbolística del malagueño, tampoco ocultó su satisfacción tras el encuentro. "Me alegro mucho por él. Viene de dos lesiones que son fracturas importantes que le han impedido tener su nivel. Va sintiendo cada vez menos dolores y no lo sobrecargamos. Está prácticamente al cien por cien. Hoy lo demostró", destacó el Ingeniero en su paso por la sala de prensa. Unas palabras que confirman tanto la mejoría física del jugador como la prudencia con la que el cuerpo técnico sigue gestionando sus esfuerzos, dándole minutos y titularidades, pero no partidos completos por el momento. Porque el objetivo no es únicamente que Isco vuelva a brillar en un encuentro concreto sino que pueda mantener la continuidad y la regularidad sobre el terreno de juego que las lesiones le han arrebatado durante tanto tiempo. "Es un líder muy importante por lo que juega y transmite. Se lo merece por el esfuerzo que ha puesto para volver", añadió el técnico chileno. Y aunque el primer objetivo es recuperar definitivamente su mejor nivel con el Betis, Isco tampoco renuncia a volver a vestir la camiseta de la selección española, sacándose la espinita de esa Eurocopa ganada por la Roja en la que no pudo estar. Así lo reconocía hace apenas unos días en una entrevista con Sport, en la que admitía la dificultad de regresar al combinado de Luis de la Fuente, pero dejaba abierta la puerta a una nueva convocatoria. "Hay una selección muy joven con mucho talento y es difícil, sobre todo porque ya tengo una edad, pero aquí estamos. Voy a intentar sacar mi mejor nivel en el Betis y ojalá poder volver a ir, no me escondo", aseguraba el malagueño, que a sus 34 años todavía conserva la ilusión de volver a ser internacional. En esa misma entrevista, Isco reconocía que las lesiones le habían enseñado "a valorar el día a día, a disfrutar de cada entrenamiento, de cada minuto que estoy dentro del campo". Y resumía con una frase especialmente significativa el momento que atraviesa después de tanto sufrimiento: "Poder jugar, poder entrenar, poder competir… ahora, gracias a mucho trabajo y a muchos momentos del gimnasio, estoy viendo la luz otra vez". Aquel Isco que abrió los ojos en 2023 en su presentación inspirada en Juego de Tronos y que, contra todo pronóstico, logró recuperar su mejor versión, aquella que le hizo brillar en el Málaga y convertirse en una estrella internacional ganándolo todo en el Real Madrid, empieza a levantarse una vez más. Y después de tantas operaciones, meses de recuperación y dolores, el Betis vuelve a disfrutar de su magia con el balón. Una gran noticia para los verdiblancos y también para LaLiga.

articles.title: Women's football: Billion-dollar boom is leaving players behind - Fifpro raises concerns
articles.summary: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress, a Fifpro survey indicates.
articles.body:
Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.

That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro. , external

Players were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated of players considering leaving the game early, 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%.

Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors.

"Players are now very visible," she said.

"Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."

While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone.

"Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.

In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.

Most women players earn less than £15,000 - Fifpro

Legal action against Fifa to include women's schedule

Women's football could become 'billion pound' industry

The report states that global revenue in the women's game is expected to rise from about $581m (£439m) in 2024 to over $1bn (£756m) in 2027.

It also highlights emerging psychological pressures facing professional women's footballers.

In an increasingly digital world, players are more accessible than ever through social media, bringing them closer to fans but also exposing them to online harassment and abuse.

The Fifpro survey suggested that although salaries, visibility and investment have risen significantly since 2017, much of the professional game still operates in precarious conditions.

For Culvin, the sport's commercial growth is not yet being matched by safeguards for the players driving it.

"The economic case for women's football has been made," she said.

"I think the institutional regulatory and policy case needs to catch up quickly to protect and enhance our women's players and enable them to perform maximally."

Players don't see themselves as 'professional'

One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.

Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.

In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.

All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.

However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football.

"Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.

The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250).

Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa.

While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.

Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.

Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.

Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income.

"Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin.

"There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."

She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.

Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.

Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".

The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.

Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality.

"I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.

One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.

In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football.

That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago.

"What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.

The report highlights a widening divide within the women's game. The sport's elite clubs and players have benefited from investment and visibility, yet much of the global workforce remains vulnerable.

"You've got an industry that's very focused on the top 5% of players," Culvin said.

"But then what you've got is the rest, which is 95% of the industry who are not paid on time, who have short contracts. They don't get paid for 12 months - they are in incredibly vulnerable and precarious environments."

Despite that, Fifpro insists the solution is not to slow down growth but to ensure that commercial success and player welfare develop together.

"There doesn't need to be a choice for those between commercial growth and player protection," said Culvin.

"Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem."

"What we're saying is enough is enough and the industry needs to react to the players' needs and centralise the players' voice, ensure that players have a seat at the table when decisions that affect them are being made about them."

articles.title: Texas has an Arch Manning Problem and 8 overreactions after Week 6 of 2026 College Football Season
articles.summary: Well, that was something.
articles.body:
Week 6 of the college football season delivered, and the fallout from the chaos and the upsets will loom large in the weeks and months to come.

We have a new, definitive No. 1 team, while one of the sport's preseason darlings saw its season finally fold. In terms of coaching, the hot seat got warmer for many, although one coach delivered a victory that is likely to make him an offseason darling.

From Lane Kiffin to Arch Manning, we're overreacting to a wild week of college football and what it all means.

Iowa (Yes, Iowa) is a Legitimate College Football Playoff Threat

On a short week, coming off a disappointing loss against Ohio State, Iowa delivered an emphatic statement at Washington.

No, Washington isn't the team we thought we were getting before the year began. But that doesn't matter. Playing with its backup QB, Iowa clobbered Washington 41-24, racking up more than 450 yards of offense on a short week.

For the Hawkeyes, they'll head into a bye week at 5-1. What's to come after the bye week, however, is where this gets interesting.

Iowa plays at Minnesota, Wisconsin, at Northwestern, Purdue, at Illinois and Nebraska to close out the year. It is possible Kirk Ferentz's team will be favored in every game moving forward, although none of them are a given.

If Iowa were to win out, it would find its way into the playoff. Period. No debate. No drama. With only one loss to one of the best teams in the country, the Hawkeyes would have a debate-free ticket to the CFP.

If the team runs the ball the way it did on Friday night for the next eight weeks, look out.

Florida State's Search for a New Head Coach Begins Now

In desperate need of a victory, Florida State was up 14-0 on Louisville and absolutely rolling. Then the rest of the game happened.

Mike Norvell's team was dominated the rest of the way, losing 44-20. For the year, the Seminoles are now 3-3.

Oh, and they travel to Miami next week. We're just going to preemptively pencil that in as a loss.

The importance of this loss cannot be overstated. For Florida State, an eight-win season looked momentarily within reach.

But now? It's hard to see another outcome but the obvious one.

FSU still plays Miami (as mentioned), Clemson, at Boston College, at Pitt, NC State and Florida. There are no sure things left, even if at least a few more victories seem likely.

At this point, Norvell's future with the program seems clear. The Seminoles were close to moving on from the head coach last year, only to pivot from that plan.

Although his buyout will still be enormous, the time is now.

Bill Belichick Has North Carolina Rolling

In a week that featured plenty of bad on the coaching front, there were also some pleasant surprises.

No coach generates more regular overreactions than Belichick, and this weekly staple has taken its fair share of takes on his tenure since he arrived.

After upsetting Pittsburgh, however, Belichick deserves love. It's clear this program has taken huge strides forward. In fact, if not for a lengthy weather delay in the game against Clemson, which flipped the feel and momentum of that game, North Carolina would be 4-1.

Even the lone loss to Notre Dame featured plenty of competitive moments.

At 3-2, North Carolina has a slew of winnable games to come. Outside of playing Miami, which will at least be played at home, the rest of the schedule is largely winnable.

Without a doubt, Belichick's tenure has been turbulent at times. Struggles on the football field along with program turbulence have made the path challenging. But it would be a disservice to not acknowledge the incredible progress being made.

For Texas, it's time for a moment of honesty.

Coming off a stunning, ugly 27-24 loss to Oklahoma, one thing has become clear. Arch Manning, who accounted for three touchdowns in the defeat, is also limiting this team's ceiling.

Indeed, Manning has progressed since early last year, where the struggles were painfully evident. But the program and offense remain limited by what Manning can—and cannot do—on the field.

The three touchdowns were solid, although the two interceptions he threw likely doomed the Longhorns.

In five games, Manning has scored 10 touchdowns and thrown five interceptions. Last season, he accounted for seven interceptions all season, and it seems likely that he'll eclipse that number soon enough.

It's not that Manning doesn't have talent; that's why this has been a constant conundrum. It's that he seems to be at his ceiling, thus limiting what the Longhorns' talented roster can ultimately accomplish.

Bob Chesney is College Football's Next Coaching Star

For programs in search of a college football coach capable of bringing them to the promise land long, look no further.

Bob Chesney, now 5-0 at UCLA, is here to help.

For now, Chesney is working miracles with the Bruins, and the program will do anything to keep it that way. UCLA just beat Oregon outright as a double-digit underdog, which changes the entire complexation of the season.

Considering how lost this program has been of late, this development is nothing short of extraordinary. Chesney's dominance at Holy Cross led him to James Madison, where he delivered a dominant 2025.

UCLA hired Chesney in hopes of finding some stability, and it's safe to say he's provided that and then some.

Here's the kicker. There isn't a game on UCLA's remaining schedule that this team can't win. The Bruins play Wisconsin, Michigan State, Nevada, at Minnesota, Illinois, at Michigan and USC to end the year.

Like Iowa, UCLA is a real threat to make the playoff.

As for Chesney, he'll likely be at the very top of the list for any team in search of a head coach this offseason. And for good reason.

The Ducks' year will continue onward. In fact, Oregon will take on a much-improved Nebraska squad next week in a matchup that feels suddenly fascinating.

But as for the College Football Playoff and the hunt for the national championship, well, that ship appears to have sailed.

Oregon's loss to UCLA is crushing for a variety of reasons. For starters, it drops the Ducks to 3-2 after five games, moving the team oh so close to that dreaded third loss. In the College Football Playoff era, teams with three losses are left out.

Even more concerning, however, is how erratic the play has been all season. Not having quarterback Dante Moore certainly hurt, especially with how poorly Dylan Raiola played in his absence.

What has become clear, however, is that the issues are far more than just the quarterback. The pieces have never felt quite right with this group, and it seems beyond saving.

As for that potential third loss, here's the kicker. Nebraska could be the team that officially knocks the Ducks out next week. Oregon also plays Northwestern and at Ohio State in back-to-back weeks, and that likely won't go well.

Officiating Aside, Georgia is the Best Team in College Football

Oh, the officials had a bad night. Let's begin there.

From odd replay reviews to missed pass interference calls to missed holding calls, the officiating for the Georgia-Alabama game was absolutely dreadful, and it felt largely one-sided, at least at times, in Georgia's favor.

With that acknowledged, give the Bulldogs credit. Winning at Alabama is enormous. Beating Keelon Russell is enormous. Staying unbeaten as the rest of the SEC destroys itself each week is, you guessed it, enormous.

Quarterback Gunner Stockton delivered a handful of incredible, clutch throws, and the Georgia running game flexed its muscles. As for the defense, it did a sensational job of containing Russell throughout the night.

We could credit the officiating for Georgia's 20-17 win; it would be difficult to disagree with that. But when we do that, we must also acknowledge and appreciate the gargantuan effort from Kirby Smart and the Bulldogs.

Lane Kiffin's Hot Seat Conversation Starts Now

Lane Kiffin isn't getting fired this year.

We shouldn't even entertain that discussion. LSU has tied itself to the coach in a robust way—especially financially—and he'll be given time to turn things around. As he should.

For as polarizing as Kiffin can be, it would be unrealistic to expect him to work the kind of miracle many expected him to work. But losing to Kentucky is the kind of loss that will make LSU boosters uneasy, even if the Wildcats seem much improved.

And entering Week 7 with two losses is less than ideal, especially with a challenging stretch of games on deck.

LSU plays Mississippi State, at Auburn, Alabama, Texas and at Tennessee over the next five games. With that in mind, it makes the loss to Kentucky that much more crippling.

Here's the reality regarding the whole "hot seat" conversation. It doesn't start and suddenly just end in most instances. It's a bad loss here, a bad loss there and an accumulation of mishaps.

This loss won't decide his tenure in Baton Rouge, but it's a mulligan he no longer has. And with more pressure on him than any coach in college football, the pressure will only continue to mount.

articles.summary: El ex del Brighton impresionó en su debut a pesar de jugar sólo 31 minutos ante el Tottenham
articles.body: No está siendo un buen comienzo de temporada para el Manchester United. Más bien, todo lo contrario. El rival del Atlético en Champions League viene de firmar su peor inicio en Premier... ¡¡¡en los últimos 40 años!!! Marchan decimoterceros después de sumar, únicamente, seis de los 18 puntos que han disputado. Un gol de Dominic Solanke en el 92' provocó que volaran dos nuevos puntos de Old Trafford, pero el empate ante el Tottenham (1-1) dejó una gran noticia para los 'diablos rojos': el debut oficial de Carlos Noom Quomah Baleba (Duala, 2004). El internacional camerunés, fichado este verano a cambio de 75,9 millones de euros, era un viejo objeto de deseo del United. Sólo las elevadas pretensiones económicas del Brighton -se descolgó pidiendo 116 millones de euros- impidieron que aterrizara un año antes en el 'Teatro de los Sueños'. "Me gusta mucho Carlos Baleba del Brighton. Creo que podría reemplazar a Casemiro. El Manchester United necesita buscar un sustituto que tenga buena forma física y la energía para recorrer todo el campo. Además, debe ser muy bueno con el balón y Baleba puede hacerlo", vaticinaba Jaap Stam, ex de los 'diablos rojos'. "Odio que me comparen con otros, pero supongo que no puedes evitar que lo hagan", reconocía Baleba allá por 2024. Sin embargo, su 'cameo' ante el Tottenham ha desatado la euforia. A pesar de disputar sólo 31 minutos -reemplazó a Youri Tielemans en el 79'-, completó una sólida actuación. El ex del Brighton fue el segundo jugador del Manchester United que más ocasiones generó (2), el cuarto que más recuperaciones registró (6) y que más balones interceptó (3), el quinto que más pases dio en el último tercio (4) y el noveno que más duelos ganó (3 de 5). "Lo hizo bien, fue bueno tenerlo en el campo. Creo que ayudó, sin duda ayudó", confesaba Michael Carrick, contrariado por el empate. El técnico del United, sin embago, ya le había visto en acción durante el parón: "Me resultó particularmente agrable ver a Baleba jugar sus primeros minutos con nuestra camiseta en el partido a puerta cerrada contra el Lausanne". Mucho más efusivo se mostró otro ex del United, Owen Hargreaves: "Algunos fichajes tardan meses, a veces incluso una temporada entera, en demostrar su valía. A Baleba le bastaron 30 minutos para demostrar por qué está aquí. Al principio, pensé que Pogba estaba en el campo. En serio, ¿de dónde salían esos balones largos? Luego ves cómo se mueve y recupera el balón, y ves a Casemiro. Parecía que teníamos a Pogba y a Casemiro en un solo jugador". "Antes de su entrada, Bruno Fernandes había desaparecido, Tielemans tenía dificultades para marcar la diferencia y Kobbie Mainoo estaba haciendo prácticamente todo el trabajo en el centro del campo. En el momento en que salió Baleba se notó el alivio. Mainoo por fin tenía a alguien que entendía el mismo patrón: recuperar el balón, recuperarlo rápidamente, mantener la posesión y hacer avanzar al equipo", insistía Hargrevas. Paul Ince, encargado de llevar las riendas del United a principios de los 90, también le otorga su bendición: "Depositar todas tus esperanzas en alguien como Baleba es una decisión muy difícil, pero lo vi mucho en el Brighton y, aunque sigo pensando que le falta pulir algunos aspectos, me gusta. Tiene buena pierna, es agresivo y puede recorrer todo el campo". El 'nuevo' Casemiro aguarda al Atlético.

articles.title: Un mal inicio en casa...¿con el ‘asterisco’ del calendario?
articles.standfirst: Los cuatro primeros rivales como anfitrión del Elche, peor local de Primera junto al Valencia, juegan en Europa
articles.summary: Los cuatro primeros rivales como anfitrión del Elche, peor local de Primera junto al Valencia, juegan en Europa
articles.body: De una temporada a otra, el Elche ha visto cómo ha cambiado drásticamente su dinámica en casa. De ser uno de los mejores locales de LaLiga EA Sports, una fuerza clave para lograr la salvación, a convertirse en el peor anfitrión (junto al Valencia). Suma un único punto en el Martínez Valero, obtenido en su último compromiso ante el Celta (0-0). Una mala cifra, clave para entender que esté al filo del descenso (a falta de los dos partidos pendientes del Levante), con seis puntos en ocho jornadas. Sin embargo, a su mal arranque como local se le puede poner un ‘asterisco’: sus cuatro primeros adversarios en el Martínez Valero disputan competición europea. Barcelona (0-5), vigente campeón de Primera; Real Sociedad (2-3), último campeón de Copa, título que le otorgó el billete para la Europa League; Real Madrid (2-3), fijo en la Champions; y Celta (0-0), que repite participación en Europa League vía Liga. Para más inri, el horizonte en casa de los franjiverdes tampoco augura demasiado respiro. Aunque su próximo contrincante en su estadio será el Valencia, penúltimo clasificado, después le esperan dos visitas de conjuntos de Champions: Betis y Atlético de Madrid. Para completar la ‘anomalía’ del calendario, el Elche cerrará la primera vuelta como local frente al Getafe, escuadra de Conference League. Entre Atleti y Getafe, recibirá al Sevilla. En resumen, siete de los nueve equipos de Primera que visitarán el Martínez Valero antes del ecuador de la Liga juegan en Europa. En la segunda vuelta, el cuadro ilicitano sólo se medirá en su feudo a un equipo que disputa competición europea: el Villarreal, de Champions. Que es, precisamente, su próximo rival, el sábado a las 16:15 horas en el Estadio de la Cerámica. Después, el Elche afrontará una segunda salida consecutiva: visitará al Rayo Vallecano, reciente finalista de la Conference League...y que jugaría en Europa si hubiera ganado aquella final. Por el lado contrario, los caprichos de este calendario pueden darle una ventaja a los franjiverdes de cara a su objetivo de seguir en Primera. En la segunda vuelta, recibirán a varios teóricos rivales directos por la permanencia: Rayo Vallecano, Levante, Dépor, Málaga, Alavés, Osasuna, Espanyol y Racing. Además de estas ocho escuadras, Villarreal y Athletic también visitarán el Martínez Valero en la segunda mitad de la campaña.

articles.title: Mou recupera su 'búnker'
articles.standfirst: El Madrid entrenará en Valdebebas antes de viajar a Roma, recuperando el método que el luso implantó para la Champions y que todo apunta a que será la norma esta temporada
articles.summary: El Madrid entrenará en Valdebebas antes de viajar a Roma, recuperando el método que el luso implantó para la Champions y que todo apunta a que será la norma esta temporada
articles.body: a Roma con los deberes hechos en Valdebebas. El Real Madrid afrontará la previa de su visita a la capital italiana de este martes con una rutina que lleva el sello de José Mourinho. En lugar de completar el entrenamiento de vísperas sobre el césped del Estadio Olímpico, como acostumbran los visitantes en la Liga de Campeones, el conjunto blanco se ejercitará en Valdebebas y volará a las 15.00 horas para aterrizar en suelo romano a las 17.15. La costumbre de entrenar en el escenario del partido es casi un rito en el fútbol europeo, pero Mourinho fue el primero en romperla en el Real Madrid. Durante su primera etapa en el banquillo blanco (2010-2013), el portugués optó por preparar los desplazamientos en la Ciudad Deportiva, una decisión que la prensa de entonces vinculó a su afán por blindar el plan de partido y proteger cualquier detalle táctico de miradas ajenas. El propio Mourinho, eso sí, no siempre ha sido fiel a su dogma. La temporada pasada, al frente del Benfica, sí se ejercitó en el estadio rival en sus visitas al Real Madrid y al Chelsea. Aquella fue, precisamente, la ocasión en la que el portugués volvió a pisar el césped del Bernabéu remodelado trece años después, pese a que llegaba sancionado y no pudo dirigir el partido del día siguiente. En el resto de sus desplazamientos europeos, sin embargo, el Benfica preparó los encuentros en su ciudad deportiva de Seixal, fiel a la filosofía que ahora recupera en Madrid. La práctica cayó en desuso con los sucesores de Mourinho. Tanto Zinedine Zidane como Carlo Ancelotti fueron partidarios de pisar el estadio rival en la víspera, fieles a la rutina clásica. El giro llegó la temporada pasada de la mano de Xabi Alonso, que recuperó el método mourinhista antes de la visita a Anfield y continuó en el resto de desplazamientos. Ahí ordenó entrenar a las once de la mañana en Valdebebas y viajar por la tarde a Liverpool, donde la expedición se trasladó directamente al hotel y solo el entrenador y un futbolista acudieron a Anfield para la rueda de prensa. El experimento, sin embargo, no echó raíces. Álvaro Arbeloa, que relevó a Xabi en el banquillo, rompió de nuevo con esa filosofía y devolvió al Madrid a la rutina tradicional de ejercitarse en el feudo contrario, como se comprobó en el Estádio da Luz en su estreno europeo lejos del Bernabéu. Ahora, con Mourinho de vuelta en la casa blanca, el búnker regresa a su origen, y todo indica que no será algo puntual. La previsión es que la rutina se convierta en norma el resto de la temporada en cada salida europea.

articles.title: Ref Watch: Why Ryan Gravenberch's first yellow card was harsh but Liverpool midfielder deserved eventual red against Man City
articles.summary: Liverpool lost 3-0 to Manchester City in the Premier League on Sunday, with Ryan Gravenberch sent off for two bookable offences; Dermot Gallagher believes the midfielder was unlucky to receive his first yellow card, but says there was no doubt about the second
articles.body:
Gravenberch was sent off with the game goalless after bringing down Jeremy Doku, in a flashpoint that shifted the momentum in City's favour. The Liverpool midfielder had been one of the standout performers for an hour before his dismissal.

Speaking on Sky Sports News' Ref Watch, Gallagher said referee Chris Kavanagh was harsh in his initial decision, believing the official mistakenly thought Gravenberch had caught Doku's knee rather than the top of his boot.

"It is really harsh [first yellow card]," Gallagher said.

"I think the problem for Chris [Kavanagh], in his view, I think he thinks that he clips his knee.

"He doesn't if you look again. He thinks he has clipped his knee, so he thinks it's a high boot and a yellow card.

"He catches the top of his boot. He is very unlucky."

Former Tottenham and Aston Villa manager Tim Sherwood agreed that the first caution was unwarranted, arguing Gravenberch had made an attempt to win the ball and pulled out of the challenge.

"I don't think that tackle should be a yellow card. It is an attempt to win the ball," Sherwood said.

"He pulls out of any kind of challenge. It is not a yellow card. You want your team to be aggressive and on the front foot."

However, Gallagher was adamant that Gravenberch's second booking was correct, pointing to the impact of the challenge rather than its severity.

"Without a doubt [yellow]. It is not about the severity of the tackle, it's about the impact. I don't think he can win that ball," he said.

"He didn't have to make the tackle. He is already on a yellow, he knows that and the referee knows that.

"The referee will think it has broken a promising attack. The learning curve of the referee is don't put yourself in the position to be under pressure.

"The first yellow puts Gravenberch and himself [the referee] under pressure."

Sherwood also accepted that the Liverpool midfielder had left himself vulnerable by attempting to stop Doku, who was able to move the ball away from the challenge.

On the second yellow, Sherwood added: "He is so quick and toes it away. It is a genuine attempt to play the ball but he puts himself on offer having already been on a yellow."

Former Premier League forward Jay Bothroyd shared the view that the first booking was soft, suggesting it ultimately spoiled a finely poised contest, but agreed that the second challenge could be punished.

"It is soft [first yellow]. That shouldn't even be a question of a yellow card, it is not for me. It ends up spoiling the game," Bothroyd said.

"The second yellow, I think it is [a booking]. He could've been on the pitch still.

"In that situation, we are talking about Doku. He is rapid and electric.

"Gravenberch thinks he can get there and then he can't. It is a promising attack. That is why he has been given the yellow.

"In isolation, I don't know if it's a yellow challenge but because it was a promising opportunity to break, that is why it has been given."

Did Haaland add pressure on Gravenberch decision?

Erling Haaland immediately approached referee Chris Kavanagh after Gravenberch's challenge on Jeremy Doku, which resulted in the Liverpool midfielder receiving his second yellow card.

The incident raised questions over whether the Manchester City striker's reaction put additional pressure on the referee, although former Premier League referee Gallagher believes Kavanagh had already made up his mind.

"He has made up his mind by that point. He wasn't throwing yellow cards around, the first one was for a technical incident," Gallagher said.

"The first yellow for a foul came in the 47th minute. Unfortunately, he picked the wrong one [Gravenberch's first]."

Former Premier League forward Jay Bothroyd suggested Haaland's immediate reaction was an attempt to influence the decision.

"In this situation, Haaland runs over straight away. He is clearly saying he needs to be sent off," Bothroyd said.

"When that happens, isn't that the same as doing that [the card gesture]."

Tim Sherwood also highlighted how quickly Haaland approached Kavanagh after the challenge, questioning whether the striker's intervention could have influenced the referee.

"As soon as he made that challenge, Haaland is sharp enough to the referee. He goes straight up to him and is almost saying, do the right thing," Sherwood said.

articles.title: Portugal makes sharp U-turn on Cristiano Ronaldo suspension, wants him back after Al-Nassr goal: Will he answer the call?
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo may return to the Portugal national team after scoring for Al-Nassr, amidst a U-turn by the Portuguese Football Federation. Will he accept the call for the upcoming international fixtures?
articles.body: Cristiano Ronaldo is back among the goals for Al-Nassr, and Portugal want their captain back. Despite the disciplinary proceedings over his departure from the national team camp, federation president Pedro Proença and coach Jorge Jesus have both explicitly said they want him to return. Ronaldo has also made clear that he remains willing to represent Portugal once the matter is resolved, but with November’s fixtures approaching, will he answer the call?Ronaldo scores for Al-Nassr as Portugal's stance softensRonaldo returned to club football on Friday, October 9, scoring the opening goal in the 23rd minute of Al-Nassr’s 3-0 victory over Diriyah Club. It was his first appearance since leaving Portugal’s national team camp during the October international break, and his 980th career goal brought the milestone of 1,000 closer as the dispute over his international future continued.Al-Nassr supporters welcomed him with a large banner reading “Greatness is earned” and chanted his name during the seventh minute, offering a show of support while his relationship with Portugal remained uncertain.The Portuguese Football Federation had initiated disciplinary proceedings on Friday, but announced the case publicly on Saturday, classifying it as urgent and referring it to the Disciplinary Investigation Committee. The federation said Ronaldo had initially been subject to an automatic provisional suspension after leaving the camp without permission, before a separate, non-automatic preventive suspension was ordered as the proceedings began.However, the public tone changed within hours, when Proença made clear that the federation wanted its captain back for the November international break.“The federation, the coach and all of Ronaldo's teammates are of one mind, we want Ronaldo back,” Proença said, in comments relayed by Italian journalist Fabrizio Romano.“I expect Ronaldo to return during the international break next November, and he is also eager to return, he is the best player of all time,” the federation president added.What happened between Ronaldo and Jorge Jesus?The fallout began when Ronaldo left Portugal’s camp on September 30 after a dispute with Jesus over his role in the team. Ronaldo had expected to play against Norway, according to his account, but remained an unused substitute despite warming up, and he subsequently accused the coach of breaking his word and failing to explain the situation honestly.Ronaldo later published a lengthy statement, initially released to Portuguese media, setting out his version of events and explaining why he felt trust had been broken. He apologised to his teammates for leaving the camp, accepted responsibility for his actions and said he was prepared to face whatever disciplinary punishment the federation considered appropriate.Crucially, he did not present the incident as an international retirement announcement. Instead, Ronaldo said he wanted to keep representing Portugal once any suspension had been served, provided he remained fit and continued playing for his club.“So, if I am physically fit, playing with my team, and hoping to score goals, after my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I have always been, to compete and win with our national team. This, believe me, is the absolute truth,” Ronaldo wrote.Jesus has also now made his position clear, indicating that the disagreement will not prevent a possible recall. His earlier response to Ronaldo’s statement was restrained, saying he had read the message and had nothing further to add, but he has since aligned himself with the federation’s conciliatory approach.“I don't know. I don't know what Cristiano might decide…Since nothing extraordinary happened that affected my authority as a coach, for me, Cristiano will be eligible for the next call-up [November] if he is playing for Al Nassr, provided that he wants to return to the national team,” Jesus said.The coach has also characterised the tension as a misunderstanding, making clear that Ronaldo would remain welcome if he wished to return and met the necessary sporting requirements.Ronaldo's 1,000-goal ambition could bring him backRonaldo has now done precisely what he said would be necessary for a return: he has resumed playing for Al-Nassr and continued scoring. His goal against Diriyah took his career tally to 980, leaving him 20 short of a landmark that could become one of the defining moments of his final years in football.Portuguese journalist Miguel Pereira previously told talkSPORT that Ronaldo wanted to score his 1,000th career goal in Portugal colours rather than for Al-Nassr, giving the milestone a potential international significance. If that ambition remains unchanged, November could offer him another opportunity to move closer to the target with his country.Portugal have already secured their place in the Nations League quarter-finals after winning their opening four matches. They face Denmark on November 14 before travelling to Wales three days later, and all eyes are now on whether Ronaldo will be back in the squad.The disciplinary proceedings are still ongoing, but with federation president Pedro Proença and coach Jorge Jesus both making it clear that they want Ronaldo back, the case may not prove to be a major obstacle to his return. articles.title: Leicester City: How silences were ended and boos were heard on another tough day for the Foxes
articles.summary: Silences were ended and boos were heard on another tough day for Leicester City as they were beaten by Robbie Savage's Peterborough United.
articles.body:
Boos, nervousness, helpless shrugs and another failure to launch.

Leicester City's latest defeat at King Power Stadium by lowly Peterborough United had Foxes boss Russell Martin saying there will be "no quick fix" in sacking him when supporters chanted for his dismissal.

Midfielder John Lundstram spoke of the team playing with "anxiety" at home, which has no doubt been exacerbated by the now regular criticism the Foxes are subjected to after a slow start to life in League One following back-to-back relegations.

That admission came at the end of a day that started with two of the club's hierarchy giving rare interviews, with long under-fire chief football officer Jon Rudkin defending the club's owners while sporting director James McCarron backed head coach Martin – albeit before this latest capitulation.

So how did the highly anticipated meeting with Peterborough, a side led by former Foxes captain Robbie Savage, go from McCarron speaking of being "super excited" to ex-winger and BBC Radio Leicester pundit Matt Piper questioning how much "respect" Leicester players have for Martin?

Leicester owners still committed to club - Rudkin

Savage's Posh beat Leicester to pile pressure on Martin

For years, media outlets had placed formal requests with Rudkin to speak about the club's fortunes – be them good or bad, from Premier League title triumphs to three relegations in four years.

That was, until just over an hour before kick-off at King Power Stadium on Saturday when he sat down with BBC Radio Leicester commentator Owynn Palmer-Atkin for an interview that lasted less than 10 minutes.

For the first time, Rudkin addressed the heavy criticism that he, along with owner Khun 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha, have been the target of for years – culminating with calls for him to leave the club and for the Foxes to be sold.

And while BBC Sport has seen the sale brochure that has been circulated, in which the club is on the market for more than £200m, Rudkin said he "cannot comment on speculation".

The game was still to kick off when sporting director McCarron also spoke to BBC Radio Leicester, more than seven months after he took the job with the Foxes.

Dominating the discussion was the state of Leicester on the pitch this season, the appointment of Martin and the rebuilding of the squad after a summer clear-out of high-earning under-performers after successive relegations.

Martin, a manager that some Foxes fans chanted their disapproval of when linked with the former Scotland international in years gone by, has endured a torrid few months at the helm with the team languishing in the bottom half of League One.

It was just minutes before they kicked off what would become their third home defeat of the season that McCarron spoke enthusiastically about what he felt the Foxes could look forward to after the extended three-week international break that allowed Martin more time infuse Leicester with the style of play he was hired for.

McCarron said he was "totally convinced" that Martin is the right manager the job.

"The central reason why we decide to appoint the manager is that we feel he can deliver a control-the-ball, dominate-territory style game with courage and intensity," McCarron said.

"But that takes time when you do 30 transfers over the summer. You need to see things settle down before you start to see the consistency."

And what McCarron saw before the defeat by Peterborough was a side he felt "should really start to take off".

15:00 BST: Failure to launch from kick-off

When the clock finally ticked down to kick-off, there was no "take-off".

Owura Edwards put the visitors ahead after just 12 minutes and Harry Leonard doubled the advantage before Warren O'Hora's own goal had Savage's little-fancied Posh 3-0 up at the break.

The former Wales international had only been in charge at Peterborough for just over a week, joining a team who prior to the game at King Power Stadium were winless in six league games.

It took the Foxes 20 attempts on goal to finally pull a goal back in the 68th minute when Emil Riis finally found the back of the net.

Many Leicester supporters had already picked up and left before that goal, and Martin was well aware of it from where he stood in the technical area.

Martin has previously spoken about how he feels criticism he has received has "become really personal".

On Saturday, he accepted the jeers, boos and shouts for him to be sacked as being a hazard of the job after another damaging defeat.

"The chants are what they are. It is what it is and we have to keep our head down and work really hard," he said.

"I have to accept the personal stuff because I'm in charge of the team ultimately, so it's my responsibility."

He did also defend himself by adding: "I'm as frustrated as any of them, but if you think changing a manager is a quick fix then I'm not sure that's ever the way."

The 40-year-old's insistence on playing possession-based, heavy-passing football, which is so often bemoaned when results go against his sides, was again the focus of post-match analysis.

However, he turned attention on to his players by saying he wanted a more aggressive performance.

"You have to weather the storm at some point and you have to suffer in a game of football," Martin said.

"Maybe for five or 10 minutes, just be ugly, just be horrible, and fight. Right now, when we have to suffer, we don't look like a team."

Piper said the performance and lack of reaction from Foxes players reflects poorly on Martin.

"He is saying 'turn the game ugly for 10 minutes' and they have clearly not got that message on the training ground," Piper said.

"And that has you question how is he delivering these messages? How is he communicating that to the group? Why are they not listening to him?"

And with Savage – a player that Piper featured alongside for the Foxes in the Premier League - getting his side performing so well instantly, the big personality and presence of the Welshman only made it look worse for Martin.

"When he wanted something to happen on the football pitch, Robbie Savage was on the football pitch and he was driving the team from the sideline. He was delivering those messages," Piper said.

"And that is when his team was winning. Russell Martin's team were losing and he's saying they are not doing the things he asked them to do, and he is turning around and shrugging at his backroom staff.

"I have to question if he is really giving those messages on the training ground, because if that is what you want from your group and they are not listening to you, then they have no respect for you mate."

Just two players - Luke Thomas and Bobby De Cordova-Reid - that featured in the draw with Hull City that condemned Leicester to relegation last season started against Peterborough.

For years, the clear-out of players on big wages to make way for younger homegrown talent to help rebuild the club is what has been called for by observers and supporters alike.

Martin has turned to youth, with Will Alves and teenagers Louis Page and Olabade Aluko a trio of relatively inexperienced academy graduates that started against the Posh.

Around them, however, was vast experience - includes once-capped England international Alex McCarthy in goal, former Italy Under-21 international Caleb Okoli starting in defence, while the midfield included Lundstram, who ended his loan stint with Hull last season by helping them earn Premier League promotion.

This, however, has done nothing to wipe away the woes of Foxes past.

"With the pressure the club's been under the last couple of years, the players just feel a little bit anxious at times," Lundstram said.

"I think a lot of us just go in our shell a little bit, which is hard because obviously all the supporters just want us to do well. They just want us to make the better decisions more often than not.

"We're all better players than what we're showing. We really are.

"When you step over the white line you need to have that bit of presence and bit of pride to show you are a top player, and I think at the minute there is a bit of nervousness."

articles.title: Florian Wirtz: Liverpool midfielder's start to life in Premier League compared as Jamie Carragher calls for him to be dropped
articles.summary: Jamie Carragher has claimed that Florian Wirtz should be dropped by boss Andoni Iraola after a poor start to the season; Sky Sports' Callum Bishop analyses what the German brings to Liverpool and how he compares to other Premier League number 10s when they first joined new clubs
articles.body:
Those were Jamie Carragher's hopes on what Florian Wirtz could've been for Liverpool. In the next breath he said "he needs to come out of the team."

To say it's been an underwhelming start to life at Anfield would be an understatement. The price tag (£116m), expectations and comparisons to the likes of De Bruyne have certainly not helped.

If the challenge ahead of Wirtz was like climbing Everest, comparing him to the best the Premier League has or had to offer when their legacies are already cemented isn't going to make life easier.

The issue is, the majority of these names made bigger impacts from the jump. Thus far, Wirtz has played 39 Premier League games since his big-money move last summer. In that time, he has averaged 0.18 assists, 0.16 goals and created 2.2 chances per 90.

Without context, these numbers mean nothing. Compare them to other players and then the problem begins to magnify. In De Bruyne's first 39 Premier League games at Man City, he far outperformed Wirtz in all three of these areas. And it's not just the Belgian.

The same can be said of Cole Palmer at Chelsea and even Martin Odegaard at Arsenal, who was equally hit with claims of a slow start to life at the Emirates.

Those defending Wirtz may argue that isn't all his fault. Assists rely on those he is feeding to finish. True, and he is in the 90th percentile of chances created among all attacking midfielders in Europe's top five leagues since the start of last season. Despite that, his assist numbers don't even put him in the 50th percentile.

However, his expected assists still pale in comparison to what Odegaard and Palmer in particular were managing in their first 39 games at new clubs.

He doesn't even rank in the top three in chances created per 90 for Liverpool this season.

In the areas you'd expect a number 10 to be elite in, Wirtz isn't hitting the mark. Is he valuable anywhere else? He's obviously not a ball-winning midfielder so that's out of the equation. What about ball progression?

Of the quartet, Wirtz ranks lowest in total carries per 90 and above only Odegaard in carry distance and carry progression. He barely cracked the top eight in progressive carries at his club last season too. So, it's not that either.

It continues to beg the question: what is Wirtz to Liverpool? He isn't a prolific goalscorer, nor a prolific playmaker. He is not relied upon to progress his team up the pitch. And the biggest worry of all? He seems to actually be getting worse.

Is Wirtz actually getting worse under Iraola?

The standards Wirtz set last season were deemed as being below par. Yet, they are better than what he is producing under Iraola.

He has dropped to the top 30 and 40 per cent in chances created and touches in the opposition box in the Premier League this season. Last season, he was in the top 10 per cent in both.

He has improved in assists, but, with the greatest respect, that's only because his one assist is a third of his total of three last term. He is marginally better with his progressive carries too, but that isn't his strength and seems more indicative of Iraola's style of play.

The reality seems to be, Wirtz hadn't adapted to English football during his first campaign. That has continued to be the case as he enters his second.

The difference now is, he has a head coach who operates with a style of football that is only going to make it harder for Wirtz to flourish. Creatively, Iraola's history has always been that chances come through his use of wingers. If you use the XI against City as an example, that falls on Bradley Barcola and Victor Munoz.

Wirtz's role in all this? Shuffle the ball on to those players.

For £116.5m, you'd expect more. That's why the criticism is what it is. And if that truly is what his role has now been reduced to, Carragher might be right.

At some point, Iraola will have to consider whether someone else can do what Wirtz is doing while offering at least a bit more defensive stability. There seems little point to judge it based on creative flair, because it appears there's even less room for that in this system.

articles.title: Michael Carrick: Manchester United head coach is in trouble ahead of crucial week against Atletico Madrid and Leeds
articles.summary: Michael Carrick faces the biggest week of his Man Utd career so far with difficult away trips to Atletico Madrid and Leeds Utd; The Red Devils are winless in five out of the last six games after conceding a late equaliser to 10-man Spurs on Saturday; Spurs remain winless in the league
articles.body:
United have failed to win five out of their last six games in all competitions - the latest being Saturday's 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham, who scored a late equaliser through Dominic Solanke.

Carrick's side now face a huge week with two tricky away trips to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday night, then a trip to high-flying Leeds United who just lost their unbeaten record to reigning champions Arsenal on Saturday.

Read below for the Magic Man's thoughts about a big week for Carrick and United...

'I haven't seen signs of improvement at Man Utd'

After Saturday's game, I'd more worried if you're a Man Utd fan. I've seen signs with Tottenham that things can improve, there's something there. I haven't seen any signs with Man Utd at the moment.

Now, Michael Carrick is in trouble over the next two games. I hope he doesn't get the sack, but he's in trouble.

It's a nightmare week for him. I couldn't think of two worse games - and I don't think they're going to win either of them.

Atletico Madrid, at their ground, it's a difficult game. They're hard to beat, a very difficult team to play against and beat. They don't let in a lot of goals.

Then you go to Leeds, who's one of Man Utd's champion enemies. This is a big, big, big football match. A big rivalry. And it's one of Leeds' biggest games.

And if you're a Leeds fan, after the weekend, you'd be shocked if Man Utd beat them at Elland Road. Every Leeds fan would be disappointed if they didn't get a result against Man Utd this weekend.

Now that's a big swing in football. How many times have we said that about Leeds vs Man utd games? And it tells you everything you need to know about Man Utd.

I've always said the same thing about Carrick. When they were playing well last season and he got them into the Champions League, everyone was saying: give him the job, give him the job.

But what I wanted to see was how he'd react when they go three or four games without a win.

It's alright when you're winning every week. You're all in, you're on a crest of a wave. Ask any manager, it's easy when you're rolling.

But how was Carrick going to handle the pressure? What was he going to do differently? We're seeing that now. It doesn't seem like he is coming up with the ideas to get out of it.

If he was like this last season, he wouldn't have got the United job permanently. But now he's got the contract.

United should have gone for Unai Emery. They should have done whatever they could to get someone like him. Someone with major experience, who has been around the block. This is a hard job.

Now, who else is going to come in? Eddie Howe is probably the man they'd go for. He's the only one about isn't he?

Antonio Conte could go in, he'd steady the ship. But I don't know if he wants to play entertaining football and set the world alight. I don't know what the Man Utd owners want.

'Spurs needed to get a proper centre forward in the summer;

Tottenham played well at Old Trafford. They dominated, but just don't look like scoring a goal at the moment.

They did great with 10 men to come back and finally get an equaliser which they deserved.

They only thing they probably could have done with - and what they should have done - is they had to get a centre forward.

They went out of their way for a few players, did a bit of this and that. I like Sandro Tonali, I'm a big fan of this. But they had to get a centre forward.

Dominic Solanke is better than alright. But he's not yet an actual goalscorer. When Spurs robbed United of the ball in the first half and he goes through on goal, you don't sit there and go: 'goal'. You just don't.

And Omar Marmoush isn't going to give you goals. He'll get you're a worldie here or there, but he's not a goalscorer. They needed a goalscorer. I can't believe Spurs didn't go for Nicolas Jackson. He's decent.

The problem with Spurs at the moment is that they're not scoring. There's never a wrong time to score - every time is the right time - but they're failing to find the net when they're on top.

They could go to Coventry on Monday Night Football , score an early goal and kick on to win 3-0 or 4-0. That could be the result that kick-starts their season."

But I've seen them plenty of times this season and they've played well - but only for 20 to 25 minutes. They need to turn that into 90.

But you have to say fair play to them for coming back at United when they're having the season they're having, they're down to ten men, dominated the game and gone 1-0 down.

articles.title: What are the key matches to watch as the UEFA Champions League returns?
articles.summary: Atletico vs Man United and Man City vs PSG headline the league’s match day two action as the competition returns.
articles.body:
The UEFA Champions League (UCL) 2026-27 enters its second round of matches this week, with 36 teams in action across Europe as clubs return to the elite football competition.

After the first set of league fixtures, two-time title holders Paris Saint-Germain lead the points table with three points, followed by six-time champions Bayern Munich and five-time winners Barcelona, who also won their opening matches.

The competition’s league phase format, now in its third year, started in September and runs until January 2027. It will be followed by the knockout rounds, with the champions crowned in early June.

Here’s all you need to know about this year’s competition:

The Champions League is an annual club competition that features the best teams from across Europe.

This season marks the third time that 36 teams will participate in the main round, an increase from 32 under the old format.

What is the 2026-27 Champions League format?

Since 2003, the UCL has featured 32 clubs split into eight groups of four, with the top two from each section advancing to the last 16.

That has changed radically in recent years.

From the 2024-25 season, the 36 clubs are pooled into a single league in a “Swiss system” more commonly associated with chess.

Earlier, participating teams played six games in the group stage, facing each opponent home and away. Now, each club plays eight games, one each against eight different opponents.

How does the Champions League knockout format work?

At the end of the league phase, the top eight qualify directly for the knockouts, while those between the ninth and 24th places have to compete in two-legged knockout-phase playoffs.

Teams ranked 25th and below are eliminated.

The UCL knockout format is straightforward – it begins with the round of 16, followed by the quarterfinals, semifinals and the final.

articles.title: Festival del Pucela, que se desmelena y amarga el estreno de Etxebe
articles.standfirst: El Albacete sufre su cuarta derrota consecutiva y sigue colista y sin ganar pese al cambio de entrenador
articles.summary: El Albacete sufre su cuarta derrota consecutiva y sigue colista y sin ganar pese al cambio de entrenador
articles.body: El Real Valladolid se desmelenó y avasalló al Albacete en el debut en su banquillo de un Joseba Etxeberria que vio cómo los suyos cayeron goleados, siendo ampliamente superados de inicio a fin. Los goles de Ponceau, David Torres, Arnu y Latasa en apenas 37 minutos, de la mano de un inspiradísimo Víctor Jr., originaron la fiesta blanquivioleta en un José Zorrilla que vio cómo Arnu repitió para redondear la manita. De este modo los de Fran Escribá encadenan cuatro jornadas sumando y dos triunfos seguidos en casa, mientras la escuadra manchega sufre su cuarta derrota consecutiva y sigue colista y sin ganar pese al cambio de entrenador. Desde el principio, los pucelanos desarbolaban a los manchegos con hambre, ganas e intensidad. De esta manera, iban cayendo los goles uno tras otro. Los dos primeros, de cabeza, anotados por Ponceau, al cabecear el centro de Thiago Ojeda tras un gran pase al hueco de Víctor Jr., y por David Torres, con otro testarazo tras un córner de Víctor Jr., para sorprender al Albacete. Con Thiago Ojeda a los mandos y Víctor Jr. en pleno crecimiento con el paso de los partidos, la máquina blanquivioleta seguía a lo suyo y también veían puerta los delanteros. Los tantos de Arnu, rematando una gran combinación entre Víctor Jr. y Ponceau, y de Latasa, a placer tras centro de Garriel, aumentaban el resultado antes del descanso, al que se llegaba con un 4-0 que incluso podía ser más amplio después del córner directo de Víctor Jr. al larguero y el balón de Arnu que se estrellaba en el palo. La única opción en la primera parte de los visitantes, que muy pronto perdieron por lesión a Fran Gámez, fue en un tiro de Víctor Valverde que también era rechazado por la madera. Lejos de saciarse y aunque dejaba maniobrar algo más al Albacete, el Pucela quería más en el segundo tiempo. Así, el disparo cercano de Arnu que taponó Lluis López y el de Latasa que Mariño neutralizó fue el preámbulo del quinto gol, al rematar Arnu en el área pequeña el buen centro de Víctor Jr. firmando así su doblete el 19 en otra buena jugada que permitía al 30 dar su segunda asistencia; incluso Víctor Jr. pudo completar su partidazo con un gol, pero no acertó por poco en dos remates con mucho peligro. A partir de entonces, el ritmo del choque bajaba y, a pesar de los cambios y de que el extremeño Daniel Miranda no concediese un posible penalti sobre Latasa, el resultado ya no variaba y el Valladolid se llevaba ante el colista tres puntos muy importantes para dar un salto en la clasificación antes de volver a jugar en el Zorrilla en la próxima jornada.
